data.name: Khaba
data.detailed_description:
A mystery puzzle adventure

Michael is an ambitious explorer searching for a secret treasure. Finding himself trapped in the dark pyramid of Khaba, a weak ray of sunlight becomes his only hope.

Through chambers filled with puzzles, Michael must reflect this beam against orbs and dusty mirrors to pass each test. When a lit stone opens one passage, another one is blocked and each chamber becomes a further test of patience and reason.

As Michael descends deeper into the pyramid, every solved puzzle will also unfold new parts of his troubled story. Almost as if the pyramid itself is testing Michael, an optional story about the dead Pharaoh will demand alternative solutions to each puzzle – but also expose the true nature of Michael’s past.

- 28 puzzle levels
- Hours of gameplay
- Voice-acting
- Alternative endings

Khaba is a game from Swedish game studio Hello There, with a thrilling story, challenging puzzles and intuitive gameplay combined in a unique mix.

data.short_description: In Khaba, you follow the explorer Michael on his quest for a treasure in a forgotten pyramid. Through chambers filled with puzzles, he descends deeper into the mysteries of the buried Pharaoh. Each chamber becomes a further test of patience and reason, revealing the true nature of Michael’s past.

reviews.review:
Khaba is a compact puzzle adventure that takes a familiar ancient Egyptian setting and builds an interesting logic game around the manipulation of light. Developed and published by Hello There Games, it follows Michael, an ambitious explorer whose search for a mysterious treasure leaves him trapped inside a dark pyramid. His only meaningful connection to the outside world is a faint ray of sunlight, and that light becomes both his means of survival and the foundation of nearly every challenge standing between him and the deeper sections of the tomb.

The main puzzle system revolves around directing beams of light through each chamber. Orbs, mirrors, stones, and other environmental devices must be positioned or manipulated so that the beam reaches the necessary destination. The concept sounds straightforward, but the game complicates matters by connecting different mechanisms together. Illuminating one stone may open a passage while simultaneously blocking another route, meaning that simply finding a way to shine light onto a target is not always enough. Players have to understand the relationships between the objects in a room and determine the proper sequence for activating them.

There are 28 puzzle levels, and the difficulty develops at a comfortable pace. Earlier chambers function as an introduction to the fundamental rules, while later areas expect a stronger understanding of how light interacts with the available mechanisms. This progression gives the game a satisfying rhythm because new challenges generally feel like extensions of ideas the player has already learned rather than completely disconnected gimmicks. Some solutions require experimentation, but the relatively contained environments make it possible to study the situation and gradually work toward the answer.

What gives the experience additional personality is the way puzzle solving connects with Michael's story. Traveling farther into the pyramid gradually reveals information about his troubled past. The structure therefore becomes more than a collection of puzzle rooms. There is a psychological quality to the journey, with the pyramid seemingly testing Michael while the player continues to uncover uncomfortable details about the person they are controlling. It is not an exceptionally elaborate narrative, but it gives purpose to the progression and provides a reason to keep descending beyond simply completing another puzzle.

An optional storyline concerning the dead Pharaoh adds another dimension. Discovering this material can require alternative solutions to puzzles, encouraging players to reconsider chambers that might otherwise appear finished. It is a clever way of integrating optional content into the core mechanics instead of relying entirely on conventional collectibles. Alternative endings further reward players willing to explore these additional possibilities. This also gives the relatively short adventure some replay value, particularly for anyone interested in seeing everything the story has to reveal.

The presentation is modest but suits the game's focused design. Ancient chambers, dusty mirrors, darkness, and beams of sunlight naturally complement one another, creating an atmosphere that feels appropriately isolated and mysterious. The graphics clearly reflect the scale and age of the production, so players expecting highly detailed modern environments will need to adjust their expectations. Nevertheless, the visual direction communicates the important information clearly, which is especially valuable in a game where understanding the position of objects and the direction of light is essential.

Voice acting is another useful addition. Since much of the experience is spent quietly considering puzzles, spoken dialogue helps provide personality and breaks up the succession of chambers. The narrative gradually becomes more significant as Michael's background is revealed, and having voiced characters makes those developments feel more substantial than simple text interruptions would have. English and German include full audio support, while subtitles broaden accessibility further.

The game's greatest limitation is also connected to its greatest strength. Khaba is extremely focused. Players searching for combat, large environments, character progression, or extensive exploration will find little of that here. The experience is fundamentally about solving environmental light puzzles while uncovering a mystery. Its 28 stages provide several hours of play, but this remains a relatively small adventure. Once the different puzzle solutions and endings have been discovered, there is limited reason to repeatedly return unless the player simply enjoys replaying logic challenges.

Performance requirements are extremely lightweight by modern standards, which makes the game accessible on modest computers. More importantly for handheld players, Khaba is Steam Deck Verified. Its functionality works with the default controller configuration, interface text is considered readable on the handheld display, and the default graphics configuration performs appropriately. It also runs successfully under SteamOS. This makes the Steam Deck a particularly convenient way to experience a puzzle game that naturally lends itself to shorter sessions.

Overall, Khaba is an enjoyable example of how a relatively simple mechanical concept can support an entire puzzle adventure when it is developed carefully. Redirecting sunlight through mirrors and other objects remains the foundation throughout, but increasingly complicated chambers, optional solutions, narrative discoveries, voice acting, and multiple endings prevent the concept from feeling completely one-dimensional. Its limited scope and dated presentation hold it back from competing with the strongest modern puzzle adventures, yet its atmosphere and thoughtful mechanics give it an identity of its own.

For players who enjoy methodical logic puzzles and mysterious ancient settings, this is an easy game to appreciate. Hello There Games created something concise rather than ambitious, and that focus works in its favor. The combination of light manipulation, interconnected mechanisms, hidden narrative material, and alternative solutions produces a satisfying experience that respects the player's ability to observe and reason.

Rating: 7/10
